ai_summary: Great Britain's wind generation currently stands at 8.0 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output delivering 2.6 GW, representing 25.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Scotland's clean power sector demonstrates remarkable environmental efficiency, registering a carbon intensity of just 2 gCO2/kWh compared to the GB-wide average of 109 gCO2/kWh. However, persistent cross-border transmission bottlenecks continue to enforce severe operational penalties. Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 5,203 MWh, accumulating constraint costs of about £93,504. To compensate for this stranded clean electricity, system operators required thermal generators elsewhere on the grid to burn an estimated 988,646 m3 of natural gas, driving an additional 1,821 tonnes CO2 in carbon emissions. Annualizing today's pace indicates an estimated total yearly curtailment cost of £34 million, which increases consumer invoices across the UK by an estimated £0.1/MWh. These figures highlight an urgent operational paradox: while Scotland generates ultra-clean electricity at near-zero carbon intensity, insufficient grid export capacity forces consumers to fund both the curtailment of renewable power and the carbon-heavy thermal energy deployed to replace it.
